# Building My Portfolio with AI Assistance

Vibe coding is redefining how people code. Imagine a super smart code assistant that guide you in your coding journey. 
With a few simple instructions in natural languages, it can create whatever you want, no need to study for years or 
working hard to learn by doing, everything working with no errors out of the box... If this sounds a bit strange and 
unrealistic, is because it is unrealistic. 

Am I starting the post of how I designed this web portfolio vibe coding, criticizing vibe coding? Yes, I am.

## Vibe coding or the new copy-pasting?

This isn't new. Everyone has searched for an easy solution on stackoverflow and copied the first comment. But nothing 
is that easy in real life. 

Using the stack overflow simil, maybe an AI can solve a puntual problem, but it can't build a hole system. And if used 
without knowledge, it can generate new errors.

## The good part of vibe-coding

However, not everything is bad. This web page was created using copilot, without any knowledge of react. Is it well coded? no.
Is it secure? no. But it is a little project that doesn't need it, a fast prototype for a futture true project.

This was done trying several AI options, investigating how they work, and learning specific tools like prompt engineering. 
And also having knowledge about deployment in github pages, basic frontend and general coding.

## Final words

Is it vibe-coding the devil? No, it's not. But I don't think is a magic wand that translates your desires into code.
Vibe-coding is a tool, and a very good one. But, as every tool, it needs a learning process. 

As everything arrownd AI, it will power up good developers, but will do no good to mediocre ones.

Lets continue learning.

posts.content:
# Designing with Empathy: Building for Real People

Design systems, component libraries, and flashy animations are nice. But they don't replace a simple habit: asking who you're building for. For small portfolios and prototypes, empathy is the secret ingredient that makes things useful instead of just pretty.

I used to treat UI as a checklist: inputs, labels, responsive grid. That approach produces functional pages, but it misses a layer — the context of the person clicking the button. Who is that user? What problem are they solving right now? Answering those questions early changes decisions dramatically.

## Tiny habits that help

- Watch someone use your page for 60 seconds. You don't need a lab — just a friend or family member.
- Write the minimum micro-copy that reduces doubt: clarify button actions, explain results briefly.
- Favor predictable behavior over cleverness. Surprises are fun for engineers; they're confusing for users.

These feel obvious, but they're easy to skip when you're excited about a new animation or a technical trick. For the leaf pathogen detection project I worked on, one small change — showing a clear "Upload one photo" hint — reduced user confusion more than a week of refactors.

## Empathy isn't soft, it's practical

People sometimes treat empathy as a soft skill that doesn't matter in technical projects. I disagree. Empathy is a pragmatic design tool: it reduces support questions, shortens onboarding, and lets features shine because they solve real problems.

A few closing thoughts: don't over-engineer the solution to appear smart. Ship something that helps someone. Iterate with real feedback. You'll write less code overall and make a better product.

Let's keep designing with people in mind.

posts.content:
# Soft Skills That Ship Features

Talking about soft skills feels vague in a technical portfolio. But over time I noticed a pattern: projects with better conversations finish faster. Meeting notes, quick demos, and small decisions saved days of rework.

## Concrete habits that help teams

- Short demos every few days. They expose assumptions early and reduce scope creep.
- Commit messages that explain "why". Future you (and your teammates) will thank you.
- Ask clarifying questions instead of assuming requirements are fixed.

These aren't glamorous, but they remove friction. In one project, a ten-minute sync avoided a week-long integration headache because we agreed on one data format early.

## Communication as engineering

Good communication is a form of engineering: it reduces uncertainty, aligns expectations, and makes trade-offs explicit. It's also low-cost to practice — add a line to a PR explaining the intent, or record a 60-second walkthrough of a tricky bug.

Soft skills don't replace hard skills. They multiply them. If you can write a clean component and explain its limits clearly, that component will actually get used.

If you're building your portfolio or collaborating on a small team, invest a little time in the conversations. The code will follow.

# Teaching and Building a Cedu Chatbot

Teaching for a year changed how I think about learning and product design. I worked one-on-one with a student for twelve months — planning sessions, breaking down concepts, and adapting explanations to fit their pace. That experience was humbling and clarifying: learning isn't a single path, it's a conversation.

During that time I began developing a small educational chatbot (I call it the "Cedu Chatbot") to help the student practice problems and review concepts between sessions. The chatbot is intentionally simple: short prompts, guided hints, and quick checks to keep confidence high and frustration low.

## What tutoring taught me

- Explain the goal first. Students ask "why" more than you expect; naming the objective keeps them engaged.
- Small wins matter. Short, solvable exercises build momentum.
- Feedback beats correctness. Showing why an answer is wrong — kindly — creates learning, not shame.

## Why a chatbot?

A chatbot extends the learning loop. It provides practice on demand, offers hints when someone is stuck, and keeps explanations consistent between sessions. It's not a replacement for human tutoring — it's a complement that scales attention when the tutor isn't available.

From a technical perspective, designing the Cedu Chatbot forced me to think about micro-interactions, prompt design, and how to surface uncertainty (when the bot should ask for clarification or suggest a human check). These are the same problems that matter in product design: trust, clarity, and graceful failure.

## Next steps

I plan to keep iterating on the bot: better hint strategies, clearer error messages, and small analytics to track progress (not to judge, but to inform the next lesson). Teaching for a year and building the bot made me appreciate the blend of empathy and engineering — both are necessary to make tools that actually help people learn.

Let's keep building tools that teach, not just test.
